title: BSNL deputy general manager urges engineering students to embrace AI, robotics and quantum technology
author: K Srinivasa Rao
content_html:
The Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (BSNL) Deputy General Manager M. Satya Prasad on Saturday (September 19, 2026) asked all students to focus on artificial intelligence, robotics and quantum technologies to enhance their knowledge and build strong career opportunities.

Along with College chairman Muttamsetti Srinivasa Rao, he inaugurated freshers’ day celebrations in Avanthi’s St. Theressa Engineering College, Garividi off Vizianagaram district. Speaking on the occasion, he said that the students of all engineering branches can focus on certificate courses of new technologies from first year itself.

The Government Polytechnic College Principal, G. Satyanarayana, said that the students must focus on practical knowledge in chosen subjects to gain confidence and come out with new ideas.

Muttamsetti Srinivasa Rao said that the management had improved infrastructure and constructed new laboratories to make students to understand new technologies and do experiments frequently. Avanthi College Principal J.Bala Bhaskara Rao, Vice Principal B.Venkata Ramana, Administrative Officer G. Anil Kumar were present.

title: Sugarcane turned bitter for thousands of farmers in North Andhra districts
author: K Srinivasa Rao
content_html:
Farmers are likely to stay away from sugarcane crops from next year, due to the closure of three sugar factories and another one on the verge of closure in North Andhra districts such as Vizianagaram, Parvatipuram and Srikakulam districts.

The farmers used to grow sugarcane in 35000 acres till about a few years ago in Vizianagaram district. Now, it has been reduced to 3500 acres. The crop area, which was around 50,000 acres in Srikakulam district got reduced to 5000 acres. The farmers are likely to shift to other crops from next Rabi season with the closure of operations in all four sugar factories.  

Lack of adequate sugarcane for crushing, continuous losses, absence of new technology for the production of ethanol and other allied products led to the closure of Sri Vijayarama Gajapathi Cooperative Sugar Factory located in Bhimasingi of Jami Mandal of Vizianagaram district. Bhimasingi sugar factory, which was established in the year 1960, closed its operations in the year 2019. Another important cooperative sugar factory located at Latchayyapeta of Seethanagaram mandal of Parvatipuram district was established in the year 1995 and was operated by NCS Group between 2002 and 2020. Due to continuous losses, the company stopped crushing five years ago.

Amadalavalasa sugar factory of Srikakulam district, established in the year 1953, stopped its operations in the year 2003. The issue of reviving the factory was an election issue every five years, but its reopening remained only on paper. Although those three sugar factories closed their operations, the private sugar factory located near Sankili of Regidi Amadalavalasa of Vizianagaram district provided much-needed relief for sugarcane farmers with its continuous operations in the last two decades. The company E.I.D.Parry India Limited informed the farmers that it might not take up crushing from next season. 

Sankili Chakkera Parisrama Parirakshana Samithi President Buditi Appala Naidu submitted a memorandum to Vizianagaram Joint Collector S.Sedhu Madhavan, requesting the government to take steps for the protection of the factory, since thousands of families depended on the factory, which provided direct and indirect employment. Lok Satta Party State President Bhisetti Babji met Minister for MSME Kondapalli Srinivas and Collector S.Ramsundar Reddy for the modernisation of the Bhimasingi sugar factory. “Closure of agro-based industries will stop economic activity in hundreds of villages located in and around the factory. In the absence of other major industries, the government should take steps for the revival of all sugar factories,” said Mr.Babji.

title: Forest department prepares proposal to develop roads to Edamalakkudy panchayat in Keralam’s Idukki
author: Sandeep Vellaram
content_html:
Amid recurring incidents of people being carried on makeshift stretchers for medical emergencies in Edamalakkudy due to lack of proper road connectivity, the Forest department has prepared a proposal to improve accessibility to the tribal panchayat. Ninestretches will be developed into all-weather roads and a bridge will be constructed as per the proposal.

According to officials, the department is planning to develop existing roads as well convert few trekking paths into motorable, all-weather roads. The department has proposed to complete the projects in two phases, with a suggestion to complete the construction of the bridge in the first phase. The proposed bridgeacross the Manaliyar river will link six settlements to Societykudy, the base of the panchayat where a panchayat office, primary health centre and a school are located.”Now, a temporary woven bamboo footbridge anchored to a Njaval tree is the only link connecting the six settlements to Societykudy,” the report said.

Prepared by High Range Circle Chief Conservator of Forests (CCF) D.K. Vinod Kumar, the report outlines a comprehensive plan to establish all-weather roads across all tribal hamlets in Edamalakkudy, which will soon be submitted to the State government alongside budgetary estimates. According to the officials, the proposal identifies key stretches that require immediate upgrade. The major stretches include an 18-km road from Eravikulam National Park (ENP) gate to Pettimudy, which is in a dilapidated condition, a 1.2-km forest path from Societykudy to Ambalaparakudy and a 3.6-km trekking path, connecting Keppakkad to Nooradikudy.

Rejects road to Mankulam

Meanwhile, addressing local demands for a new route connecting Koodallarkudy to Anakulam in Mankulam, the department argued that the project is unnecessary and driven by vested interests. In his report, the CCF said that the community members primarily sought all-weather access to the Munnar–Udumalpet road. “All essential public facilities, including health care, public distribution system, and schools, are located in and around Societykudy. Community representatives expressed satisfaction with the proposed link between Koodallarkudy and Societykudy. The demand for a Mankulam–Koodallarkudy route is being pushed by outsiders exploiting the tribal community,” the report stated.

Landslip risk

“Moreover, the area fromKoodallarkudy to Mankulam is extremely steep and cutting a road through it is impractical and risks triggering severe landslips and ecological disasters,” according to the report.

Munnar Forest Range Officer S. Biju said that once the proposed roads and bridges are built, they will finally guarantee dependable, all-weather connectivity for the tribal panchayat.

title: Keralam deploys digital tracking system to ensure zero expiry of donated blood units
author: Dhinesh Kallungal
content_html:
Even as the Keralam government is reportedly making moves to restructure the Kerala Development and Innovation Strategic Council (K-DISC), formed during the tenure of the previous government, including reducing its staff strength, the State’s strategic think tank and advisory body has developed a unique digital platform that tracks blood units across the transfusion chain, preventing donated blood from expiring unused.

Implemented for the first time in a State in the country, the system digitally tracks the journey of blood from the moment it is collected from a donor through processing and storage at blood banks to its final transfusion into a recipient, creating a continuous digital record across the transfusion chain.

Titled Blood Bank Traceability System (BBTS), it digitally links all public-sector blood banks in the State and tracks every unit from collection to transfusion.

According to a senior K-DISC officer, the system has helped ensure that no donated blood unit expires during collection, storage, transportation or transfusion. It also enables blood banks to follow the ‘earliest expiry, first out’ principle, ensuring that units nearing their expiry date are issued first.

Temperature monitoring

Blood is normally stored at 2–6°C, and deviations from the prescribed temperature during storage or transportation can compromise its quality. The BBTS monitors temperatures in real time and alerts authorities to technical issues or disruptions in the blood supply chain, if any, the officer said.

“Implementation of the project has been completed across government health-care institutions in Keralam, covering 87 centres in 14 districts, including 43 blood collection centres and 44 blood storage centres. This is the first phase. In the second phase, private blood banks in the State could also be brought under the platform. We have recommended this, as it requires policy-level intervention by the State government,” the officer said.

The system has been implemented in association with the Kerala State Blood Transfusion Council (KSBTC), Kerala State AIDS Control Society, e-Health and the Health department.

Digital records

It also creates continuous digital records of every stage of the blood’s journey, including collection, processing, storage, issue and transfusion along with details of donors.

The platform is also linked to ‘Jeevadhaara’, which enables voluntary donors to register and maintain their donation and health history digitally. It provides information on blood stocks and helps facilitate the availability of required blood groups during emergencies.

Real-time information on blood units available across blood banks in the State can also be accessed through the platform, enabling quicker identification and allocation of blood where it is urgently required.

title: Rising cost of metals, falling demand spell trouble for Bidriware
author: Nagesh Prabhu
content_html:
Bidriware, the centuries-old metal craft unique to Bidar and renowned for its distinctive black-and-silver finish, is facing fresh pressure from the rising prices of silver, copper, and zinc.

Artisans and small-scale producers say the sharp increase in input costs, coupled with declining demand, is squeezing their margins and threatening the sustainability of the traditional craft.

 Prices of these commodities fluctuate on a daily basis. | Photo Credit: K. Bhagya Prakash

Bidriware is made primarily from a zinc-copper alloy, while silver is used for intricate inlay work. With the prices of these metals rising sharply over the past two years, the cost of producing each piece has increased substantially.

Rising metal prices

Silver prices have risen from about ₹95,700 a kg in 2024 to ₹4 lakh in January 2026, before stabilising at around ₹2.50 lakh. Copper prices have increased from ₹750 a kg in 2024 to around ₹1,450 in 2026, while zinc prices have risen from ₹230 to around ₹400 a kg. Prices of these commodities fluctuate on a daily basis. Artisans largely source these materials from Hyderabad and Secunderabad.

During a visit to Bidar, several artisans and shopkeepers told The Hindu that they were finding it difficult to pass the entire increase in input costs on to customers, particularly in the price-sensitive domestic market. The resulting squeeze has affected both demand and their profit margins.

The characteristic deep-black lustre is produced using soil sourced from the historic Bidar Fort. | Photo Credit: K. Bhagya Prakash

Bidriware pieces typically contain about 90% zinc and 10% copper, with silver used for the intricate inlay. Craftsmen engrave delicate floral and geometric patterns on the surface and inlay silver into them. The characteristic deep-black lustre is produced using soil sourced from the historic Bidar Fort. The soil is added to a chemical solution during the final stage of the process, giving the metal its distinctive black finish.

How designs are etched

The designs are first sketched on the surface using a sharp metal stylus. The craft is used to make over 200 varieties of products, including hookahs, goblets, wall and table plates, decorative figurines, flower vases, caskets, jewellery, and table lamps.

The craft is used to make over 200 varieties of products, including hookahs, goblets, wall and table plates, decorative figurines, flower vases, caskets, jewellery, and table lamps. | Photo Credit: K. Bhagya Prakash

Artisans say corporates from Bengaluru, Mumbai, and Delhi continue to place bulk orders for customised decorative pieces, particularly as gifts for weddings and festivals or for display in offices. | Photo Credit: K. Bhagya Prakash

Abdul Basith, manufacturer and owner of Bidri Craft in Bidar, said the rising price of silver was particularly difficult for artisans because even a small quantity used for inlay could substantially increase the cost of a product.

Umar Khayam, another artisan, said some producers were being forced to consider using less silver, making smaller products or adopting less elaborate designs to contain costs. Such measures, he said, could affect the traditional character and craftsmanship of Bidriware.

Corporate orders

Artisans said corporates from Bengaluru, Mumbai, and Delhi continue to place bulk orders for customised decorative pieces, particularly as gifts for weddings and festivals or for display in offices. Foreign tourists have also traditionally been an important market.

However, the number of foreign buyers visiting Bidar has declined sharply since the COVID-19 pandemic, said Abdul Bari, another artisan.

Depending on their size and quality, Bidriware products are generally priced between ₹2,500 and ₹50,000.  | Photo Credit: K. Bhagya Prakash

Depending on their size and quality, Bidriware products are generally priced between ₹2,500 and ₹50,000. Shopkeepers said their annual business has fallen from an average of about ₹50 lakh to ₹20 lakh because of declining demand and rising metal prices.

The craft is also facing a generational challenge. Artisans form a distinct community, with nearly half belonging to the older generation. | Photo Credit: K. Bhagya Prakash

The craft is also facing a generational challenge. Artisans form a distinct community, with nearly half belonging to the older generation. Younger people are reluctant to enter the profession because income is uncertain and work depends heavily on orders, which are not regular, said Mr. Basith.

Labour-intensive

The detail-intensive craft, believed to have originated during the 15th-century Bahmani Sultanate, is highly labour-intensive.

The detail-intensive craft, believed to have originated during the 15th-century Bahmani Sultanate, is highly labour-intensive. | Photo Credit: K. Bhagya Prakash

With the number of skilled craftsmen falling to fewer than 75, artisans and shop owners have urged the State government to establish a dedicated training centre to provide skill-based training to unemployed youth and help preserve the craft. | Photo Credit: K. Bhagya Prakash

Even a small vase can require up to 10–12 days of work. With the number of skilled craftsmen falling to fewer than 75, artisans and shop owners have urged the State government to establish a dedicated training centre to provide skill-based training to unemployed youth and help preserve the craft.
